title: Microorganisms and Disease
description: Grade 8 Biology: Microorganisms and Disease — concept notes, solved examples, key-point recaps, per-topic quizzes and free online tests.

topics.title: Types of Microorganisms
topics.concept:
All around us, and even inside our own bodies, live tiny living things that are far too small to be seen with the naked eye. These are called microorganisms or microbes, and they can be seen only with the help of a microscope. Microorganisms are found almost everywhere — in air, water, soil, food, and on and inside the bodies of plants and animals. Despite their tiny size, they play an enormous role in nature, in our health, and in industry. The study of these tiny organisms is called microbiology.

Microorganisms are classified into five major groups. Bacteria are extremely small, single-celled organisms with no true nucleus; they come in shapes like rods, spheres, and spirals, and reproduce very rapidly by simply splitting in two. Viruses are even smaller than bacteria and are unusual because they can reproduce only inside the living cells of a host (a plant, animal, or even a bacterium); outside a host they are inactive, which is why scientists place them on the borderline between living and non-living.

The remaining three groups are larger and more complex. Fungi include single-celled forms such as yeast and many-celled forms such as moulds and mushrooms; the greenish or blackish growth on stale bread or rotting fruit is a fungus. Protozoa are single-celled, animal-like microbes such as Amoeba and Paramecium, and some, like the malaria-causing organism, are harmful. Algae are simple, plant-like microbes that contain chlorophyll and make their own food by photosynthesis; examples include the green threads (Spirogyra) seen floating in ponds.

Microorganisms can be both useful and harmful to us. Some help in making curd, bread, and medicines, and in keeping the soil fertile, while others cause diseases in humans, plants, and animals, and spoil our food. Because they are present everywhere and multiply so quickly, understanding the different types of microorganisms is the first step to using the helpful ones and protecting ourselves from the harmful ones — the central theme of this chapter.

examples.problem: Example 1: What are microorganisms, and how can we see them?
examples.solution:
Recall the definition.

  • Microorganisms are living things too small to be seen with the naked eye.
  • They can be seen only with the help of a microscope.
  • Answer: Microorganisms (microbes) are tiny living organisms visible only under a microscope.
examples.answer: Microorganisms (microbes) are tiny living organisms visible only under a microscope.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name the five major groups of microorganisms.
examples.solution:
List the main types.

  • The groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and algae.
  • Answer: The five groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and algae.
examples.answer: The five groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and algae.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why are viruses considered to be on the borderline between living and non-living?
examples.solution:
Think about how viruses reproduce.

  • Viruses can reproduce only inside the living cells of a host.
  • Outside a host they are inactive and behave like non-living particles.
  • Answer: Because viruses are active and reproduce only inside a host cell but are inactive outside, they lie between living and non-living.
examples.answer: Because viruses are active and reproduce only inside a host cell but are inactive outside, they lie between living and non-living.

recap:
• Microorganisms (microbes) are living things too small to see without a microscope; they are found in air, water, soil, food, and living bodies.
  • The five major groups are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa, and algae.
  • Bacteria are single-celled with no true nucleus; viruses reproduce only inside a living host.
  • Fungi (yeast, moulds, mushrooms) and protozoa (Amoeba, Paramecium) are larger microbes; algae make their own food by photosynthesis.
  • Microbes may be useful (curd, bread, medicines, soil fertility) or harmful (diseases, food spoilage).

quiz.q: Microorganisms can be seen only with the help of a:
quiz.explanation: Microbes are too small for the naked eye and need a microscope to be seen.

quiz.q: Which microorganism can reproduce only inside a living host cell?
quiz.explanation: Viruses are active and reproduce only inside a host cell.

quiz.q: Which group of microbes makes its own food by photosynthesis?
quiz.explanation: Algae contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise like green plants.

quiz.q: Amoeba and Paramecium are examples of:
quiz.explanation: Amoeba and Paramecium are single-celled, animal-like protozoa.

quiz.q: The fuzzy growth on stale bread is a:
quiz.explanation: The mould on bread is a fungus that grows in warm, damp conditions.

topics.title: Useful Microorganisms
topics.concept:
Although we often blame microbes for disease, a great many of them are extremely useful and are essential for life on Earth. One of the most important services microbes provide is in keeping soil fertile through nitrogen fixation. Plants need nitrogen to grow, but they cannot use the nitrogen gas in the air directly. Certain bacteria, such as Rhizobium, live in the root nodules of leguminous plants (peas, beans, gram) and convert atmospheric nitrogen into compounds the plant can absorb. Some free-living soil bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) also fix nitrogen, naturally enriching the soil.

Microbes are also nature's great recyclers through decomposition. Bacteria and fungi break down the dead bodies of plants and animals, and other organic wastes, into simple substances that mix back into the soil. This decomposition clears away dead matter and returns nutrients to the soil, keeping the cycle of nature going. Without decomposer microbes, dead leaves, bodies, and waste would pile up everywhere and the nutrients locked inside them would never be released for new life.

In our kitchens and food industries, microbes help make many foods and products. The bacterium Lactobacillus turns milk into curd, multiplying in warm milk and changing it into a thick, tasty, easily digestible food. Yeast, a fungus, is used to make bread rise: it ferments the sugar in the dough, releasing carbon dioxide gas that forms tiny bubbles and makes the bread soft and spongy. Microbes are also used in making cheese, idli and dosa batter, and many other fermented foods, as well as in producing alcohol.

Perhaps the most life-saving use of microbes is in making medicines, especially antibiotics. Antibiotics are substances produced by certain fungi and bacteria that can kill or stop the growth of disease-causing microbes; the famous antibiotic penicillin comes from a fungus. Microbes are also used to prepare vaccines, which protect us from many serious diseases. From enriching the soil, to recycling waste, to making food and medicine, useful microorganisms quietly support our daily lives in countless ways.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which bacterium fixes nitrogen in the root nodules of legumes?
examples.solution:
Recall the nitrogen-fixing microbe.

  • Leguminous plants have root nodules containing helpful bacteria.
  • These bacteria, called Rhizobium, fix atmospheric nitrogen.
  • Answer: Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants.
examples.answer: Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen in the root nodules of leguminous plants.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does yeast help in making bread?
examples.solution:
Think about fermentation.

  • Yeast ferments the sugar in the dough.
  • This releases carbon dioxide gas, which forms bubbles and makes the bread rise and become soft.
  • Answer: Yeast ferments sugar in the dough, releasing carbon dioxide that makes the bread rise and turn soft and spongy.
examples.answer: Yeast ferments sugar in the dough, releasing carbon dioxide that makes the bread rise and turn soft and spongy.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is an antibiotic, and name one example.
examples.solution:
Recall the meaning and an example.

  • An antibiotic is a medicine made from microbes that kills or stops the growth of disease-causing microbes.
  • A well-known example is penicillin, made from a fungus.
  • Answer: An antibiotic is a microbe-derived medicine that kills or stops harmful microbes; penicillin is one example.
examples.answer: An antibiotic is a microbe-derived medicine that kills or stops harmful microbes; penicillin is one example.

recap:
• Many microbes are useful: they fix nitrogen, decompose waste, make food, and provide medicines.
  • Rhizobium bacteria in the root nodules of legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil.
  • Decomposer bacteria and fungi break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
  • Lactobacillus turns milk into curd; yeast ferments dough to make bread rise; microbes also make cheese and other fermented foods.
  • Antibiotics (such as penicillin) and vaccines are made using microbes to fight and prevent disease.

quiz.q: The bacterium that fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules is:
quiz.explanation: Rhizobium lives in legume root nodules and fixes atmospheric nitrogen.

quiz.q: Milk is converted into curd by:
quiz.explanation: Lactobacillus bacteria turn warm milk into curd.

quiz.q: Yeast makes bread rise by releasing the gas:
quiz.explanation: Yeast ferments sugar and releases carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise.

quiz.q: Penicillin, an antibiotic, is obtained from a:
quiz.explanation: Penicillin is produced by the fungus Penicillium.

quiz.q: Microbes that break down dead matter and recycle nutrients are called:
quiz.explanation: Decomposer bacteria and fungi break down dead matter into soil nutrients.

topics.title: Harmful Microorganisms
topics.concept:
While many microbes are helpful, a number of them are harmful because they cause diseases and spoil our food. Microorganisms that cause disease are called pathogens. Harmful microbes affect not only humans but also plants and animals, and the diseases they cause can spread from one individual to another. Pathogens belong to all the major groups: some diseases are caused by bacteria, some by viruses, some by fungi, and some by protozoa.

In humans, harmful microbes cause many familiar diseases. Bacteria cause illnesses such as tuberculosis (TB), cholera, and typhoid; viruses cause the common cold, influenza (flu), measles, and polio; the protozoan that causes malaria is spread by mosquitoes; and certain fungi cause skin diseases like ringworm. These pathogens enter the body through air, water, food, or contact, multiply inside us, and damage the body, producing the symptoms of illness.

Harmful microbes also attack plants and animals, which is a serious problem for farmers. Plant diseases such as citrus canker (caused by bacteria) and rust of wheat (caused by a fungus) reduce crop yields and can ruin harvests. In animals, microbes cause diseases such as foot-and-mouth disease in cattle and anthrax. These diseases lower food production and cause heavy losses, so controlling harmful microbes in farming is very important.

Apart from causing disease, harmful microbes also cause food spoilage. When bacteria and fungi grow on food, they break it down, change its taste, smell, and appearance, and make it unfit to eat. Spoiled food often develops a bad odour, mould, or a slimy surface, and eating it can lead to food poisoning because some microbes release harmful toxins. This is why food must be stored properly and preserved. Understanding harmful microbes helps us take steps — through cleanliness, safe food handling, and treatment — to protect our health and our food.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is a pathogen?
examples.solution:
Recall the meaning.

  • Some microbes cause disease.
  • A disease-causing microbe is called a pathogen.
  • Answer: A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease.
examples.answer: A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name one human disease caused by bacteria and one caused by a virus.
examples.solution:
Match diseases to their microbes.

  • Tuberculosis (or cholera/typhoid) is caused by bacteria.
  • The common cold (or flu/measles) is caused by a virus.
  • Answer: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria; the common cold is caused by a virus.
examples.answer: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria; the common cold is caused by a virus.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why does food go bad if it is not stored properly?
examples.solution:
Think about microbe growth.

  • Bacteria and fungi grow on unprotected food and break it down.
  • They change its taste and smell and can release harmful toxins, making it unsafe to eat.
  • Answer: Microbes grow on the food, spoil it, and may produce toxins, so improperly stored food goes bad.
examples.answer: Microbes grow on the food, spoil it, and may produce toxins, so improperly stored food goes bad.

recap:
• Disease-causing microbes are called pathogens; they harm humans, plants, and animals.
  • In humans, bacteria cause tuberculosis, cholera, and typhoid; viruses cause colds, flu, measles, and polio; a protozoan causes malaria.
  • Plant diseases such as citrus canker (bacteria) and wheat rust (fungus) reduce crop yields.
  • Harmful microbes also spoil food by breaking it down and releasing toxins, which can cause food poisoning.
  • Cleanliness, safe food handling, preservation, and treatment help protect us from harmful microbes.

quiz.q: A disease-causing microorganism is called a:
quiz.explanation: Microbes that cause disease are called pathogens.

quiz.q: Which disease is caused by a protozoan?
quiz.explanation: Malaria is caused by a protozoan spread by mosquitoes.

quiz.q: Rust of wheat, a plant disease, is caused by a:
quiz.explanation: Wheat rust is caused by a fungus.

quiz.q: Eating spoiled food can cause food poisoning because microbes release:
quiz.explanation: Spoilage microbes break down food and release harmful toxins.

quiz.q: The common cold and influenza in humans are caused by:
quiz.explanation: Colds and flu are caused by viruses.

topics.title: Communicable Diseases
topics.concept:
Some diseases can spread from an infected person to a healthy person; these are called communicable diseases (or infectious diseases). They are caused by pathogens — bacteria, viruses, protozoa, or fungi — that pass from one individual to another in various ways. Examples include the common cold, tuberculosis, cholera, typhoid, and malaria. Diseases that cannot spread from person to person, such as those caused by poor diet, are called non-communicable diseases; this topic focuses on the communicable ones.

Communicable diseases spread through several modes of transmission. Some spread through the air: when an infected person coughs or sneezes, tiny droplets carrying microbes are released, and a healthy person who breathes them in can catch the disease. Tuberculosis (TB) and the common cold spread this way. Others spread through water: when drinking water is contaminated with sewage or microbes, diseases like cholera and typhoid spread to those who drink it.

Diseases can also spread by contact and through vectors. Contact transmission happens when a healthy person touches an infected person, or shares their towels, utensils, or other belongings; many skin diseases spread this way. A vector is an animal — often an insect — that carries pathogens from one person to another without itself falling ill. The female Anopheles mosquito is the vector for malaria, and houseflies can carry microbes from waste to food, spreading diseases like cholera and typhoid.

Knowing how communicable diseases spread helps us prevent them. We can cover the mouth and nose while coughing or sneezing, drink only clean or boiled water, wash hands before eating, avoid sharing personal items with the sick, and control disease-carrying vectors by keeping surroundings clean and not letting water collect (where mosquitoes breed). Vaccination protects against many such diseases. By breaking the chain of transmission, we can stop these diseases from spreading through a community.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is a communicable disease?
examples.solution:
Recall the definition.

  • A communicable disease can spread from an infected person to a healthy person.
  • It is caused by pathogens that pass between people.
  • Answer: A communicable disease is one that spreads from an infected person to a healthy person through pathogens.
examples.answer: A communicable disease is one that spreads from an infected person to a healthy person through pathogens.

examples.problem: Example 2: Name two diseases that spread through contaminated water.
examples.solution:
Recall water-borne diseases.

  • Cholera spreads through contaminated water.
  • Typhoid also spreads through contaminated water.
  • Answer: Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated water.
examples.answer: Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated water.

examples.problem: Example 3: What is a vector? Give an example.
examples.solution:
Recall the meaning and an example.

  • A vector is an animal, often an insect, that carries pathogens from one person to another.
  • The female Anopheles mosquito is a vector that spreads malaria.
  • Answer: A vector carries pathogens between people; the Anopheles mosquito is a vector for malaria.
examples.answer: A vector carries pathogens between people; the Anopheles mosquito is a vector for malaria.

recap:
• Communicable (infectious) diseases spread from an infected person to a healthy one through pathogens.
  • They spread by four main routes: air, water, contact, and vectors.
  • Tuberculosis and the common cold spread through air; cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated water.
  • A vector (like the Anopheles mosquito for malaria, or houseflies for cholera/typhoid) carries pathogens between people.
  • Prevention includes covering coughs, drinking clean water, washing hands, controlling vectors, and vaccination.

quiz.q: A disease that spreads from an infected person to a healthy one is called:
quiz.explanation: Communicable diseases spread between people through pathogens.

quiz.q: Tuberculosis mainly spreads through:
quiz.explanation: TB spreads through air in droplets from coughing or sneezing.

quiz.q: Cholera and typhoid are commonly spread through:
quiz.explanation: Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated drinking water.

quiz.q: The vector that spreads malaria is the:
quiz.explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito carries the malaria parasite.

quiz.q: Which is a good way to prevent water-borne diseases?
quiz.explanation: Boiling drinking water kills microbes and prevents water-borne diseases.

topics.title: Immune System
topics.concept:
Our body is constantly exposed to harmful microbes, yet most of the time we stay healthy. This is because the body has a powerful defence network called the immune system, which recognises invaders and destroys them. The immune system has two lines of defence. The first is innate (inborn) immunity, which we are born with; it acts the same way against all invaders and includes barriers like the skin, the mucus lining our nose and throat, stomach acid, and white blood cells that swallow up microbes. It is non-specific, meaning it attacks any germ in the same general way.

The second line is adaptive (acquired) immunity, which the body develops over time as it meets different microbes. Unlike innate immunity, it is specific — it produces a tailored defence against each particular microbe and, importantly, it remembers that microbe. Any substance that the body recognises as foreign and that triggers an immune response is called an antigen; microbes and their parts carry antigens on their surface. When the body detects an antigen, the immune system swings into action against it.

In response to an antigen, special white blood cells produce defensive proteins called antibodies. Each antibody is shaped to lock onto a particular antigen, like a key fitting a lock. By binding to the antigen, antibodies neutralise the microbe or mark it for destruction. After the infection is over, the body keeps memory cells that remember that antigen, so if the same microbe attacks again, the body produces antibodies much faster and we may not even fall ill. This is why we usually get diseases like chickenpox only once.

This memory is the basis of vaccination. A vaccine contains dead or weakened microbes, or their harmless parts, carrying the antigen but unable to cause the disease. When a vaccine is given, the immune system makes antibodies and memory cells against that antigen, just as it would for a real infection — but without the illness. Later, if the real microbe enters the body, the immune system is already prepared and destroys it quickly. Vaccination has helped control and even wipe out deadly diseases, making the immune system one of the body's most remarkable protectors.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is the immune system?
examples.solution:
Recall its role.

  • The body has a defence network against harmful microbes.
  • This network recognises and destroys invading microbes.
  • Answer: The immune system is the body's defence network that recognises and destroys harmful microbes.
examples.answer: The immune system is the body's defence network that recognises and destroys harmful microbes.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is the difference between an antigen and an antibody?
examples.solution:
Compare the two terms.

  • An antigen is a foreign substance (on a microbe) that triggers an immune response.
  • An antibody is a protein the body makes to lock onto and neutralise a specific antigen.
  • Answer: An antigen triggers the response; an antibody is the protein made to fight that specific antigen.
examples.answer: An antigen triggers the response; an antibody is the protein made to fight that specific antigen.

examples.problem: Example 3: How does a vaccine protect us from disease?
examples.solution:
Think about training the immune system.

  • A vaccine has dead or weakened microbes that carry the antigen but cannot cause disease.
  • It makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells, so the body is ready to fight the real microbe quickly.
  • Answer: A vaccine trains the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells, so the real microbe is destroyed quickly later.
examples.answer: A vaccine trains the immune system to make antibodies and memory cells, so the real microbe is destroyed quickly later.

recap:
• The immune system is the body's defence network that recognises and destroys harmful microbes.
  • Innate (inborn) immunity is non-specific and includes barriers like skin, mucus, and microbe-engulfing white blood cells.
  • Adaptive (acquired) immunity is specific and develops memory of microbes it has met.
  • An antigen is a foreign substance that triggers the response; antibodies are proteins that lock onto and neutralise a specific antigen.
  • Vaccination uses dead or weakened microbes to make the body produce antibodies and memory cells, giving protection without illness.

quiz.q: The body's defence network against microbes is the:
quiz.explanation: The immune system recognises and destroys harmful microbes.

quiz.q: Which is part of innate (inborn), non-specific immunity?
quiz.explanation: The skin is a non-specific barrier of innate immunity.

quiz.q: A foreign substance that triggers an immune response is a/an:
quiz.explanation: An antigen is the foreign substance that triggers the immune response.

quiz.q: Proteins that lock onto a specific microbe to neutralise it are:
quiz.explanation: Antibodies are made to bind a specific antigen and neutralise the microbe.

quiz.q: A vaccine protects us by making the body produce antibodies and:
quiz.explanation: Vaccines create memory cells (and antibodies) for fast future defence.

topics.title: Antibiotics
topics.concept:
Antibiotics are medicines used to fight diseases caused by bacteria. They are special substances, originally produced by some microbes themselves, that can kill bacteria or stop them from growing and multiplying inside the body. The discovery of antibiotics is one of the greatest achievements in medicine. In 1928, the scientist Alexander Fleming accidentally noticed that a mould (the fungus Penicillium) growing on a dish had killed the bacteria around it. From this mould came the first antibiotic, penicillin, which went on to save millions of lives.

Antibiotics work by attacking parts or processes that bacteria need to survive — for example, by damaging the bacterial cell wall or interfering with how bacteria make the substances they need. Some antibiotics kill bacteria outright, while others simply stop them from multiplying so that the body's immune system can clear the remaining ones. Because they target features special to bacteria, antibiotics can fight a bacterial infection without harming the patient's own cells.

A very important point is that antibiotics work only against bacteria, not against viruses. Diseases like the common cold, flu, and measles are caused by viruses, so taking antibiotics for them does no good — viruses do not have the bacterial features that antibiotics target. Taking antibiotics unnecessarily for viral illnesses wastes the medicine and can do harm. Antibiotics should be taken only when a doctor prescribes them for a bacterial infection, and the full course should always be completed, even if the patient starts feeling better.

A growing danger today is antibiotic resistance, also called antimicrobial resistance (AMR). When antibiotics are overused or misused — taken when not needed, or stopped halfway through a course — some bacteria survive and become resistant, meaning the antibiotic can no longer kill them. These resistant bacteria multiply and spread, making infections much harder to treat. To slow AMR, we must use antibiotics only when truly needed, exactly as prescribed, and always finish the full course. Using antibiotics responsibly keeps these life-saving medicines working for everyone.

examples.problem: Example 1: What are antibiotics used for?
examples.solution:
Recall their purpose.

  • Antibiotics are medicines that fight infections caused by bacteria.
  • They kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying.
  • Answer: Antibiotics are medicines used to kill bacteria or stop their growth, treating bacterial diseases.
examples.answer: Antibiotics are medicines used to kill bacteria or stop their growth, treating bacterial diseases.

examples.problem: Example 2: Who discovered penicillin, and from what?
examples.solution:
Recall the discovery.

  • Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.
  • He found it was produced by the mould (fungus) Penicillium.
  • Answer: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, produced by the fungus Penicillium.
examples.answer: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928, produced by the fungus Penicillium.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is it useless to take antibiotics for the common cold?
examples.solution:
Identify the cause of a cold.

  • The common cold is caused by a virus, not a bacterium.
  • Antibiotics work only against bacteria, so they have no effect on viruses.
  • Answer: Because the cold is caused by a virus and antibiotics work only against bacteria, they cannot cure it.
examples.answer: Because the cold is caused by a virus and antibiotics work only against bacteria, they cannot cure it.

recap:
• Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from multiplying, treating bacterial diseases.
  • Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from the fungus Penicillium.
  • Antibiotics work by attacking features unique to bacteria, so they do not harm the body's own cells.
  • Antibiotics work only against bacteria, not viruses, so they are useless for colds, flu, and measles.
  • Overuse and misuse cause antibiotic resistance (AMR); use antibiotics only as prescribed and finish the full course.

quiz.q: Antibiotics are medicines used to fight diseases caused by:
quiz.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth.

quiz.q: The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by:
quiz.explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

quiz.q: Penicillin is produced by a:
quiz.explanation: Penicillin comes from the fungus Penicillium.

quiz.q: Taking antibiotics for a viral cold is useless because antibiotics:
quiz.explanation: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so they cannot cure a viral cold.

quiz.q: Overuse and misuse of antibiotics leads to:
quiz.explanation: Misuse lets bacteria survive and become resistant, causing AMR.

topics.title: Food Preservation
topics.concept:
Food is spoiled mainly by microbes — bacteria and fungi — that grow on it, break it down, and make it unfit and unsafe to eat. Food preservation is the set of methods we use to stop or slow the growth of these microbes so that food stays fresh and edible for a longer time. Microbes need warmth, moisture, and air to grow, so most preservation methods work by removing one of these or by killing the microbes already present. Preserving food prevents waste, keeps food safe, and lets us store and transport it across seasons and places.

Some methods preserve food using heat and cold. Pasteurisation is used for milk: the milk is heated to a certain temperature for a short time and then cooled quickly; this kills most harmful microbes without spoiling the taste, and the milk keeps longer. Refrigeration keeps food in a cold fridge, where the low temperature greatly slows down the growth of microbes, so items like vegetables, milk, and cooked food stay fresh for several days. Freezing slows microbes even more, preserving food for much longer.

Other methods work by changing the conditions microbes need. Pickling preserves vegetables, fruits, and meats by storing them in salt, oil, vinegar, or spices; the high salt or acid content stops microbes from growing, which is how pickles, jams, and similar foods last for months. Canning seals food inside airtight cans or jars after heating, so that no microbes can get in or survive, allowing food to be stored for a long time. Dehydration (drying) removes the water from food — as in dried grains, pulses, and dried fruits — and since microbes cannot grow without moisture, dried food keeps well.

A more modern method is irradiation, in which food is exposed to controlled radiation that kills microbes and pests without making the food harmful or radioactive; it is used for spices, onions, and some other foods to extend their shelf life. Common salt and sugar are also used as natural preservatives — salting fish and meat, and adding sugar to make jams and squashes, both stop microbial growth. By choosing the right preservation method, we can keep food safe, reduce wastage, and enjoy seasonal foods all year round.

examples.problem: Example 1: What is food preservation?
examples.solution:
Recall the meaning.

  • Food is spoiled by microbes that grow on it.
  • Food preservation uses methods to stop or slow microbe growth so food stays edible longer.
  • Answer: Food preservation is the use of methods to stop or slow microbial growth so that food stays fresh and safe for longer.
examples.answer: Food preservation is the use of methods to stop or slow microbial growth so that food stays fresh and safe for longer.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does refrigeration help preserve food?
examples.solution:
Think about temperature and microbes.

  • A refrigerator keeps food at a low temperature.
  • Cold greatly slows the growth of microbes, so food stays fresh longer.
  • Answer: Refrigeration keeps food cold, which slows microbial growth and keeps food fresh for longer.
examples.answer: Refrigeration keeps food cold, which slows microbial growth and keeps food fresh for longer.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why does dried food, like grains and pulses, last a long time?
examples.solution:
Think about what microbes need.

  • Drying (dehydration) removes the water from the food.
  • Microbes cannot grow without moisture, so dried food does not spoil easily.
  • Answer: Because drying removes moisture, and microbes cannot grow without water, so dried food keeps for a long time.
examples.answer: Because drying removes moisture, and microbes cannot grow without water, so dried food keeps for a long time.

recap:
• Food is spoiled by microbes (bacteria and fungi); preservation stops or slows their growth to keep food safe and fresh.
  • Pasteurisation heats milk and cools it quickly to kill most harmful microbes without spoiling taste.
  • Refrigeration and freezing use cold to slow or stop microbial growth.
  • Pickling (salt, oil, vinegar), canning (airtight and heated), and dehydration (removing water) all change conditions so microbes cannot grow.
  • Irradiation uses controlled radiation to kill microbes safely; salt and sugar also act as natural preservatives.

quiz.q: Food preservation mainly works by stopping the growth of:
quiz.explanation: Preservation stops or slows the microbes that spoil food.

quiz.q: Milk is made safe and longer-lasting by heating and quick cooling, a method called:
quiz.explanation: Pasteurisation heats milk briefly and cools it fast to kill microbes.

quiz.q: Refrigeration preserves food by:
quiz.explanation: Cold temperatures slow microbial growth, keeping food fresh longer.

quiz.q: Drying food (dehydration) preserves it because microbes cannot grow without:
quiz.explanation: Removing moisture prevents microbes from growing in dried food.

quiz.q: Sealing heated food in airtight tins for long storage is called:
quiz.explanation: Canning seals heated food airtight so no microbes can enter or survive.

questions.q: Microorganisms can be seen only with the help of a:
questions.explanation: Microbes are too small for the naked eye and need a microscope to be seen.

questions.q: Which microorganism can reproduce only inside a living host cell?
questions.explanation: Viruses are active and reproduce only inside a host cell.

questions.q: Which group of microbes makes its own food by photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Algae contain chlorophyll and photosynthesise like green plants.

questions.q: Amoeba and Paramecium are examples of:
questions.explanation: Amoeba and Paramecium are single-celled, animal-like protozoa.

questions.q: The fuzzy growth on stale bread is a:
questions.explanation: The mould on bread is a fungus that grows in warm, damp conditions.

questions.q: The bacterium that fixes nitrogen in legume root nodules is:
questions.explanation: Rhizobium lives in legume root nodules and fixes atmospheric nitrogen.

questions.q: Milk is converted into curd by:
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus bacteria turn warm milk into curd.

questions.q: Yeast makes bread rise by releasing the gas:
questions.explanation: Yeast ferments sugar and releases carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise.

questions.q: Penicillin, an antibiotic, is obtained from a:
questions.explanation: Penicillin is produced by the fungus Penicillium.

questions.q: Microbes that break down dead matter and recycle nutrients are called:
questions.explanation: Decomposer bacteria and fungi break down dead matter into soil nutrients.

questions.q: A disease-causing microorganism is called a:
questions.explanation: Microbes that cause disease are called pathogens.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by a protozoan?
questions.explanation: Malaria is caused by a protozoan spread by mosquitoes.

questions.q: Rust of wheat, a plant disease, is caused by a:
questions.explanation: Wheat rust is caused by a fungus.

questions.q: Eating spoiled food can cause food poisoning because microbes release:
questions.explanation: Spoilage microbes break down food and release harmful toxins.

questions.q: The common cold and influenza in humans are caused by:
questions.explanation: Colds and flu are caused by viruses.

questions.q: A disease that spreads from an infected person to a healthy one is called:
questions.explanation: Communicable diseases spread between people through pathogens.

questions.q: Tuberculosis mainly spreads through:
questions.explanation: TB spreads through air in droplets from coughing or sneezing.

questions.q: Cholera and typhoid are commonly spread through:
questions.explanation: Cholera and typhoid spread through contaminated drinking water.

questions.q: The vector that spreads malaria is the:
questions.explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito carries the malaria parasite.

questions.q: Which is a good way to prevent water-borne diseases?
questions.explanation: Boiling drinking water kills microbes and prevents water-borne diseases.

questions.q: The body's defence network against microbes is the:
questions.explanation: The immune system recognises and destroys harmful microbes.

questions.q: Which is part of innate (inborn), non-specific immunity?
questions.explanation: The skin is a non-specific barrier of innate immunity.

questions.q: A foreign substance that triggers an immune response is a/an:
questions.explanation: An antigen is the foreign substance that triggers the immune response.

questions.q: Proteins that lock onto a specific microbe to neutralise it are:
questions.explanation: Antibodies are made to bind a specific antigen and neutralise the microbe.

questions.q: A vaccine protects us by making the body produce antibodies and:
questions.explanation: Vaccines create memory cells (and antibodies) for fast future defence.

questions.q: Antibiotics are medicines used to fight diseases caused by:
questions.explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth.

questions.q: The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered by:
questions.explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

questions.q: Penicillin is produced by a:
questions.explanation: Penicillin comes from the fungus Penicillium.

questions.q: Taking antibiotics for a viral cold is useless because antibiotics:
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so they cannot cure a viral cold.

questions.q: Overuse and misuse of antibiotics leads to:
questions.explanation: Misuse lets bacteria survive and become resistant, causing AMR.

questions.q: Food preservation mainly works by stopping the growth of:
questions.explanation: Preservation stops or slows the microbes that spoil food.

questions.q: Milk is made safe and longer-lasting by heating and quick cooling, a method called:
questions.explanation: Pasteurisation heats milk briefly and cools it fast to kill microbes.

questions.q: Refrigeration preserves food by:
questions.explanation: Cold temperatures slow microbial growth, keeping food fresh longer.

questions.q: Drying food (dehydration) preserves it because microbes cannot grow without:
questions.explanation: Removing moisture prevents microbes from growing in dried food.

questions.q: Sealing heated food in airtight tins for long storage is called:
questions.explanation: Canning seals heated food airtight so no microbes can enter or survive.
